title: Attention Sinks as Spectral Spikes: A Mechanism Analysis of Gated Attention
claim: Adding an output gate consistently lowers spectral concentration and sink alignment while raising effective rank across layers.
layout: 4 line plots in a row, shared layer x-axis, blue vs red
description: A single horizontal strip of four line plots, each with Layer (0–28) on the x-axis. Every plot compares Pre-Gate (blue line with markers and a light blue confidence band) against Post-Gate (red line with markers and a light red band). (a) Outlier mass, the fraction of eigenvalue mass above the MP edge: blue stays around 0.65–0.75 while red drops to about 0.5–0.65. (b) Leading eigenvalue λmax of C: blue is higher, at about 30–60, and red is lower, with a dashed black line for the MP edge near zero. (c) Effective rank: red is much higher, at about 150–250, than blue, at about 70–150. (d) Sink alignment: blue spikes in early layers up to about 0.55, red stays lower, and a dashed random baseline k/T sits near zero. Captions sit under each panel. The eye goes to the blue and red gap in each panel.
caption: Post-SDPA gating suppresses token-space spectral structure. (a) Outlier mass above the MP edge decreases. (b) The leading eigenvalue moves closer to the MP edge. (c) Effective rank increases. (d) Sink-subspace alignment Alignsink(C) decreases after gating; the dashed line shows the random-subspace baseline (layer-wise mean of k/T).
abstract: Transformer attention exhibits attention sinks, where a small subset of source tokens absorbs disproportionate attention mass across layers. Recent work shows that post-SDPA output gating strongly reduces attention-sink behavior, while separate studies link attention sinks to gradient sinks and massive activations through backward training dynamics. Yet how the same gate affects forward sink structure, backward gradient concentration, and training-time representation signatures remains unclear. We address this gap by formulating attention sinks as sink-induced low-rank modes in token-space covariance, with directions aligned to high-mass attention columns. Under this view, post-SDPA gating acts as a mode-dependent contraction: it attenuates sink-induced spectral energy in the forward pass and locally reduces value-path gradients routed through sink columns in the backward pass. Empirically, random-matrix diagnostics show that gating reduces outlier mass, weakens sink-subspace alignment, and increases effective rank, while backward analyses show active-gate attenuation of first-token value gradients. Training-time diagnostics further show that gating suppresses the co-emergence of attention concentration, value-gradient amplification, and representation dominance.
